items.q: How much does custom software development cost?
items.schemaAnswer: Our typical rate is around 70 EUR/USD per hour, but pricing depends on the project. Ongoing work can be hourly or monthly, smaller scoped projects can use an initial fee and final delivery payment, and larger scopes can be split by milestones. Before estimating, we define workflows, technical risks, architecture direction, and a realistic delivery range.

answer.text: Our typical rate is around 70 EUR/USD per hour, but we do not force every project into the same pricing model.

items.schemaAnswer: Most focused MVPs take 8 to 14 weeks, depending on feature complexity, product clarity, integration depth, and security or compliance needs. We move quickly without creating throwaway foundations.

items.q: Do you work with clients outside the USA and Europe?
items.schemaAnswer: Yes. ARG is remote-first and works with teams across regions. For hybrid mode, recurring on-site sessions, or a different collaboration rhythm, we assess the setup case by case. What matters is clear written context, direct technical conversations, predictable async updates, and enough overlap for decisions.

answer.text: Yes. ARG is remote-first and works with teams across regions. What matters is not location, but whether the communication rhythm supports serious engineering work.
If you need a specific hybrid mode, recurring on-site sessions, or a different collaboration setup, we assess that case by case before promising it.
If the problem is clear and the ownership is real, distance is not the blocker.

items.q: Do you work with startups or established companies?
items.schemaAnswer: Both. We support startups building launch-ready products, companies modernizing fragile systems, teams scaling performance or reliability, and organizations building internal platforms. The common thread is technical ownership, not company size.

items.q: How do you ensure scalability and code quality?
items.schemaAnswer: Quality starts before implementation. We make architecture boundaries, testing strategy, code reviews, CI/CD, observability, recovery paths, security, and data constraints explicit so the software can evolve instead of being rewritten after year one. Testing tools vary by stack, but common choices include Jest, Cypress, Playwright, Testcontainers, xUnit, and NUnit.
